title: Short Track Cornering Technique: Crossovers, Lean and the Inside Hand Down
thumbnail_text: Stop losing speed in every short track corner

scenes.heading: Short Track Cornering Technique
scenes.sub: Lean, crossovers and a light inside hand
scenes.narration: This video shows you how to corner faster and more safely in short track. You will learn the four things that make a good corner, the mistakes that cost you speed, and what to check when your blades slip out. Short track is skated anticlockwise on a tight oval, so almost half of every lap is spent turning left. That makes the corner the core skill of the sport. It is also where races are decided. The skaters who carry speed through the bend and come out ready to attack are the ones who move to the front. This guide is for skaters who can already skate the oval and want more from the bend.

scenes.heading: Four things, in this order
scenes.chapter: The four parts of a corner
scenes.narration: Good cornering comes down to four things, done in this order. First, drop into a low position before you reach the bend. Second, lean your whole body and both blades towards the centre of the turn. Third, keep both legs pushing with crossovers all the way round. Fourth, let the inside hand brush the ice as a balance reference, not a support. Get those four right and the corner stops being the part of the lap you survive. It becomes the part where you gain.

scenes.heading: Lean with your whole body
scenes.narration: It all starts with body position. Bend deeply at the knees and hips so your hips sit low over the ice. Keep your chest calm and your head up. Look through the exit of the corner, not down at your feet. This front view shows the lean. Your whole body tips towards the centre of the turn, so your body and skates tip left together, like a motorcycle taking a bend. Your weight drives down through the inside edges. The lean is what lets your edges bite. If you stay upright, your blades cannot grip and you slide wide. So commit to the lean and trust the edges to hold you.

scenes.heading: The crossover from above
scenes.narration: You do not coast through a short track corner. You power through it with crossovers. Here we are looking down on the corner. On a left turn, your right foot lifts, travels over the left skate, and sets down on its inside edge. As it lands, it takes your weight and starts its own push. At the same time, your left leg pushes out and slightly back from underneath, then recovers under your body for the next stroke. The left push is a real power stroke, not a glide. Press the whole blade into the ice and extend the leg fully. Timing is everything. Cross too early and your feet tangle. Cross too late and you lose drive. Practise slowly at first, then build speed.

scenes.heading: When the inside hand goes down
scenes.narration: Through the deepest part of the corner, most skaters place the left hand lightly on the ice. It is not there to hold you up. It is a light touch that tells you where the ice is and helps you commit to the lean. You are brushing the ice, not leaning on it, because pressing down scrubs speed. Timing matters too. As the diagram shows, the hand comes down as you settle into the apex and lifts as you rise for the exit. Do not reach early on entry, and do not drag it onto the straight. Keep it just behind and inside your body. Low friction glove tips help the hand slide, and cut resistant gloves protect you near other skaters' blades.

scenes.heading: The last two strides before the bend
bullets: Turn your head to the exit
Rushed first crossover means you were late
scenes.narration: Most corners are lost before you reach them. If you arrive tall, drifting and still deciding where to go, the first third of the turn gets spent on corrections instead of speed. Use the last two strides on the straight to finish three jobs. Set your line. Finish getting low, so your hips are at corner height and your knees are loaded. And turn your head, so your eyes are through the bend before your skates get there. Your shoulders and hips follow your eyes. Here is a simple check. If your first crossover feels rushed or cramped, you were late. Start your lean one stride earlier for a few laps and see if the corner feels roomier.

scenes.heading: Entry, apex and exit
scenes.narration: Think of the corner in three parts. On entry, you arrive already low and already leaning, with your line set. At the apex, the tightest point of the turn beside the block, you are at maximum lean. Your crossovers are flowing and your inside hand grazes the ice. On exit, you rise slightly, direct your energy forward, and accelerate onto the straight with your eyes already up the track. The skater who gets all three parts right carries the most speed onto the straight.

scenes.heading: Why your blades slip out
scenes.narration: A blade that washes out mid corner is the most common complaint in short track. There are four causes, and you should check them in this order. First, your body. Being too upright is by far the most common cause for a developing skater, because the edge has almost no angle to bite. Film one corner from the side and from behind. Second, your edges. Draw a fingernail lightly across the edge, never along it. A crisp edge catches the nail. Third, your blade setup, meaning bend, rocker and alignment. Change one thing at a time. Fourth, the ice. Soft, late session ice gives less grip, so carry a little less speed and apply pressure smoothly. A setup change made too early hides what your body is doing.

scenes.heading: Common mistakes and fixes
bullets: Leaning with the upper body only
Pressing hard on the inside hand
scenes.narration: Most lost time comes from a short list of habits. Fix them one at a time. Standing too tall shrinks your lean, so hold a low position for one full corner, even if you skate slower. Looking down pulls your shoulders in, so pick a point at the exit and hold your eyes there. Leaning with the upper body only gives you the look of a lean without the edge angle, so tip from the ankles and hips together. Pressing hard on the inside hand takes weight off the blades, so practise with the hand hovering just above the ice. Rising early on the exit throws away speed, so stay low until your skates point down the straight. And if you cross over too early, slow the pattern down until each push finishes.

scenes.heading: Drills to train your corner
bullets: Hand hover, then light touch laps
Video from the side and above
scenes.narration: Corners improve with focused practice. Give each drill a few sessions before moving on. Start with slow laps, thinking only about a clean crossover pattern. Then do low holds, staying in your deepest position from entry to exit. Next, trace the corner with your inside hand just off the ice, then add gentle contact through the apex only. After that, drive the first four strides onto the straight as hard as you can, and watch whether you stand up to do it. Finally, film yourself from the side and from above. If your ankle is sharply painful, swollen or numb rather than simply tired, stop skating and see a physiotherapist or doctor.

scenes.heading: Get low, lean in, push both legs, touch lightly
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: So, to sum up. Get low and set your line before the bend. Lean your whole body so the edges can bite. Push with both legs through every crossover. And let the inside hand brush the ice, never carry your weight. When your blades slip, check your body first, then your edges, then your setup, then the ice. The full guide on the LiveLica blog covers how your boots, blades and gloves support your cornering, plus answers to common questions. The link is in the description.
